assignment: Your principal has decided that all students must participate in at least one extracurricular activity. For example, students could participate in sports, work on the yearbook, or serve on the student council. Do you agree or disagree with this decision? Use specific details and examples to convince others to support your position.
essay_1:
I agree with the principal that every student should have to do at least one extracurricular activity. Some people say it will take time away from homework or make kids do stuff they dont like. But I think it will help students way more than it hurts them. Activities teach you things you cant learn in class, they make you feel like you belong at school, and they help you figure out what you actually like.

First, activities teach you stuff you cant really get from a textbook. Like if you play soccer you learn you have to go to practice even when its freezing out and nobody wants to run. If you do yearbook you learn about deadlines because the pages have to be done by a certain day no matter what. Kids in student council learn how to talk in front of people and listen when people complain and also compromise when not everybody agrees. Colleges and jobs want people who can do that stuff. A lot of kids would never practice it if they just went to class and then went home.

Second, activities make students feel like they belong. A big school can be really lonely, especially if your new or shy. When you join something like chess club or drama, all of a sudden there are people who expect to see you and they notice if your not there. My cousin moved to a new town in ninth grade and didnt know anybody. She only joined cross country because a teacher kept bugging her about it, but by October she had a whole group of friends to sit with at lunch. Also kids who feel connected to there school usually get better grades and dont skip as much.

Third, if its required, kids might find out they like things they never even thought about. Alot of teenagers dont try new things because there nervous or they think they will be bad at it. But if everyone has to pick something, a kid who thinks he hates writing might find out he loves taking pictures for the school newspaper. That could even change what he wants to do when hes older.

But the rule should be kind of flexible. Some students have jobs or have to help out there family, so they should get options that fit there schedule. And there should be enough choices so everybody can find something they like. If the school does that, then I think the principal made a good choice and I hope other students support it to.
essay_2:
I agree with the principal's decision that every student has to do at least one extracurricular activity. Some people worry it will take time away from homework or make kids do stuff they don't want to do. That is a real problem, but I still think the rule does more for students than against them. Activities teach skills that classes can't, they connect students to the school, and they help kids figure out what they care about.

First, activities teach things you can't get from a textbook. On a soccer team you learn that showing up to practice matters even when it is freezing and nobody wants to run. If you work on the yearbook, you learn to meet deadlines because the pages have to go to the printer on a certain date no matter what. Student council members have to speak in front of a group, listen to complaints, and compromise when people disagree. Colleges and jobs look for these skills. A lot of students would never practice them if they just went to class and went home.

Second, activities make students feel like they belong somewhere. A big school can be really lonely, especially if you are new or shy. When you join the chess club or the drama crew, you have a group of people who expect to see you and notice when you are gone. My cousin moved to a new town in ninth grade and didn't know anyone. She was not happy for the first few weeks. She only joined the cross country team because a teacher pushed her, but by October she had people to sit with at lunch. Students who feel connected to school usually keep their grades up and skip less.

Third, a rule like this makes kids try things they would never pick on their own. Lots of teenagers stay away from new things because they are nervous or think they will fail. If everyone has to pick something, a kid who thought he hated writing might end up taking photos for the school newspaper. That could change what he studies later.

The rule could cause problems if it is too strict. Some students have jobs or have to babysit their siblings after school, and forcing them into a club would be unfair. There also need to be enough choices so nobody gets stuck in something they dread. But if the school fixes those issues, I think the rule will be really good for everyone. Kids will find friends, learn new skills, and maybe even discover something they love. The principal made a smart call, and I am glad.
